newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-ITALY AWAITS CLASH OF CHAMPIONS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-ITALY AWAITS CLASH OF CHAMPIONS.

text.p: Giancarlo Antognoni played 75 matches for Italy, helped his country conquer the 1982 World Cup and holds a record that few would envy.
The Fiorentina forward is the most-capped Italy international never to win the league title. Nobody else comes even remotely close.
It is hard to avoid the conclusion that, while earning undying admiration for his loyalty, for success he should perhaps have moved to Juventus or AC Milan.
The clubs meet in Milan on Sunday for a league match between greats whose fame towers over Italian soccer as the San Siro stadium looms over its surroundings.

One can argue that there are lies, damned lies and statistics. But the figures point unerringly to the fact that the road to glory in Italian football is a signposted super-highway heading to Turin or Milan.
Between them, they have more than a third of all Italian titles since 1898 and more than half of the last 30 years.
Of the 10 most capped players in Italy's history, seven played for one club or the other.
The first ever international goal scored by an Italian player was by Milan's Pietro Lana in Milan in 1910. The 1,000th was provided by Christian Vieri of Juventus last week.
Need more proof? Look at the starting line-up for Wednesday's Italy v Poland World Cup qualifier. Seven of the nine Italian-based players are from Juventus or Milan.
Paolo Maldini is one of several "Milanisti" with the schizophrenic task of having to defend Angelo Peruzzi's goal on Wednesday and then attack it on Sunday.
There are few greats in the roll of honour of the past century or so who have not played for one or both.

Names like Dino Zoff, Omar Sivori, Giampiero Boniperti, Fabio Capello, Tarcisio Burgnich, Roberto Bettega, Marco Tardelli, Paolo Rossi, Gaetano Scirea, Claudio Gentile, Gianluca Vialli and Roberto Baggio for Juventus.
Or Cesare Maldini, Jose Altafini, Gianni Rivera, Fabio Capello, Giovanni Trapattoni, Carlo Ancelotti, Franco Baresi, Paolo Maldini, Paolo Rossi and Roberto Baggio at Milan.
Not to mention the foreign luminaries -- Jimmy Greaves, John Charles, Nils Liedholm, Gunnar Nordahl, Liam Brady, Michel Platini, Marco Van Basten, Ruud Gullit.
Juventus have won the league "scudetto" a record 23 times and Milan 15, four of them in the last five seasons.
Internazionale Milan, with 13 titles, are the only other club with double figures and also the money to match. But they have won only three titles in the last 30 years.
Milan, unusually far behind in seventh place, currently wear the league shield on their shirts as champions while European Cup holders Juventus are set to take it back.
For once, the final clash of the year between the two protagonists will not be a title playoff.
Six points clear at the top and with a European Cup semifinal next week, Juve will not want to slow their march towards a 24th title in the club's centenary year.
But, with veteran Franco Baresi still marshalling the players in defence, Milan are back from the brink.

It is easy to see Sunday's match as a clash of cultures or as a handover between old and new, with the "Old Masters" Milan bowing to the supremacy of the "Old Lady" and her old money provided by the Agnelli family of Fiat fame.
But that would be only a part of the story.
Juventus may be 100 years old this year but they are as dynamic and forward-looking as any in the land.
Milan, built by media mogul Silvio Berlusconi's billions into Italy's top team of the late 1980s, may have been almost unrecognisable for much of this season.
But that hides the fact that they have world class internationals from a fistful of countries -- players that the rest of the world's clubs would love to lure away.
It would not be wise to write off a proud club that has captured the European Cup three times since 1989 and which is busy rebuilding again under coach Arrigo Sacchi.
Inter-Juventus is sometimes called the Italian derby because they are the only clubs never to have been relegated in their history. But Milan-Juventus is the real thing.
Between them, the two clubs command the loyalties of more than half the country's football fans and have the sort of spending budgets that most clubs dream of.
For the most part, the history of Juventus and Milan is about silverware. Lots and lots of trophies.
They have no fewer than 79 between them -- 43 to Juventus and 36 to Milan -- although Juve have won the European Cup just twice compared with five times for Milan.
Just one title would have been enough for Antognoni.
